## Life table

Confirm the selected cohort is large and stable enough to support a
trustworthy survival curve, and not distorted by an enrollment anomaly such
as a pandemic-era dip. The candidates are below: the selected cohort is the
one with the longest observed follow-up that clears the minimum cell size of
`r spec_min_cell(spec)`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cohorts
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate entry cohorts"
#| eval: !expr have_cohorts
ft_check1_cohorts(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr no_cohorts
cat("> **No candidate cohorts.** ", res$meta$note, "\n", sep = "")
```


The life table below reads one row per year in status. Column **A** is the
number of students still classified at the start of that year; **B** those
observed to exit at its end; **C** those who disappear from the data at its
end. **D** and **E** are those two as rates of the students actually at risk
that year, and **F** accumulates exits against the original cohort.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-life-table
#| tbl-cap: !expr if (have_life_table) paste0("Life table, ", res$meta$cohort, " cohort") else "Life table"
#| eval: !expr have_life_table
ft_check1_life_table(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr no_life_table
cat("> **No life table.** ", res$meta$note, "\n", sep = "")
```

## Exit curves

Column **F** as a picture: the share of the entry cohort observed to have
exited by each year in status. The dashed line marks the state's maximum
timeline, which is where "exited within the timeline" is read off. The grey
line is the at-risk estimate described in the next section, with its
confidence interval; where the two run together, nobody had left the data
yet.

```{r}
#| label: fig-exit-curve
#| fig-cap: !expr if (have_curve) sprintf("Cumulative exit rate, %s cohort. Censored students are not exiters, so the observed line is a lower bound. The interval covers sampling variability in this cohort's exit rates; it says nothing about whether this cohort stands for any other.", res$meta$cohort) else "Cumulative exit rate"
#| eval: !expr have_curve
plot_exit_curve(res$exit_curve, spec, survival_est = res$survival_est)
```

Splitting the same curve by the band a student started in asks whether exit
timing is already set at entry. Everything counted on this page is built on
the **`r spec_headline_label(spec)`** --- the score this state reports as a
student's overall English language proficiency result --- and a student's
band is their level on it in the first year they sat the annual assessment.
That band is derived here from the score itself, not read from a delivered
column.

```{r}
#| label: fig-exit-curve-band
#| fig-cap: !expr sprintf("Cumulative exit rate by initial ELP band, from each student's first annual %s level. Bands below the minimum cell size are suppressed and not drawn. Students with no annual score -- alternate-form takers, whose levels are on a different scale -- are shown separately rather than folded into a band.", spec_headline_label(spec))
#| eval: !expr have_band_curve
plot_exit_curve(res$exit_curve_by_initial_band, spec)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr no_band_curve
cat("> **No split by initial band.** ", res$meta$band_note, "\n", sep = "")
```

## How long, and how many

Column **F** answers "how many have exited by now" against the cohort as it
started, so every student lost along the way holds it down: it is a lower
bound. Beside it sits the standard discrete-time estimate, which compounds
each year's at-risk rate to ask what share *would* have exited had nobody
been lost. Neither is the right number alone, so both are shown.

Only the estimate carries a confidence interval, and only the estimate should.
The observed column is not an estimate of anything --- it is a count against a
denominator that quietly includes students nobody is following any more ---
and putting an interval around it would advertise precision about the wrong
quantity. The interval covers sampling variability in this cohort's own exit
rates. It is not a claim that this cohort speaks for the next one.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-survival
#| tbl-cap: "Exit rates by year in status. The observed share counts against the cohort as it started; the estimate allows for students no longer being observed, and is the only column an interval belongs to."
#| eval: !expr have_survival
ft_check1_survival(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr have_survival
gap <- res$survival_est$CUM_EXIT_EST - res$survival_est$CUM_EXIT_OBS
if (all(is.na(gap) | abs(gap) < 1e-9)) {
  cat("The two columns agree exactly here, which they do only when nobody",
      "leaves the data before the window's edge. On a real delivery they",
      "will separate, and the gap is the price of censoring.\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr have_survival
y <- res$years_to_50
for (i in seq_len(nrow(y))) {
  cat(sprintf("- **%s:** %s\n", y$BASIS[i],
              if (y$REACHED[i]) sprintf("half the cohort has exited by year %d in status.", y$YEARS_TO_50[i])
              else "half the cohort had not exited inside the window."))
}
```

Where the cohort stood when the window closed:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-timeline
#| tbl-cap: "Outcomes against the timelines. The first three rows are nested, each a subset of the one below; the last three -- exited, still classified, disappeared -- account for every student once."
#| eval: !expr have_timeline
ft_check1_timeline(res)
```

## Model 1 --- the fitted baseline

Everything above this line is descriptive: counts, and arithmetic on counts.
Where the curve was split by initial band, that was a way of grouping
students, not a variable in a model.

Model 1's other half fits the same thing, so that Model 2 has something to be
measured against. It runs in two steps.

**Unconditional --- no covariate at all.** The odds of exiting in each year in
status, and nothing else. This is the life table written as a model, and it
should agree with the life table exactly: the fitted annual hazards *are*
column **D**. Nothing new is learned here; what it provides is the baseline
every later term is added to.

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr have_model1
cat(check1_model1_note(res), "\n")
```

**Adding where the student started.** The same model with the student's
**first** `r spec_headline_label(spec)` score --- the one they entered on,
fixed for their whole run --- as a single covariate. It asks whether entry
proficiency already sets exit timing.

It is deliberately *not* the current year's score. The exit rule is applied to
that year's result, so a model of exit on it would restate the rule rather
than test anything, and every other covariate beside it would be conditioned
on the outcome's own cause.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model1
#| tbl-cap: "Discrete-time hazard model with the entry score as the only covariate. The ratio is per standard deviation of entry score; each year in status carries its own term."
#| eval: !expr have_model1_baseline
ft_check1_model1(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr have_model1_baseline
cat(check1_model1_baseline_note(res), "\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model1-dropped
#| tbl-cap: "Rows the model could not use. Nothing here is imputed."
#| eval: !expr have_model1_baseline
ft_check1_model1_dropped(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr no_model1_baseline
cat("> **No entry-score model.** ", res$meta$model1_note, "\n", sep = "")
```

## Model 2 --- does achievement predict who exits?

Model 1 describes *when* students exit. Model 2 asks a different question:
once you already know where a student started in English, does knowing last
year's content score tell you anything more about whether they exit this
year? If it does, something other than the language test is shaping who
leaves EL status --- the selection effect this stage exists to catch at the
source.

The number to read is the ratio on prior-year achievement. At 1 it adds
nothing. Away from 1 in either direction, it adds something it should not.

Both covariates are measured *before* the decision they are used to predict:
the language score at entry, the content score a year back. That is what
makes the question answerable. Put the current year's language score in
instead and the model would be conditioning on the exit rule itself, and this
ratio would be driven to 1 no matter what was true.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model2
#| tbl-cap: "Discrete-time hazard model on the person-period frame. Ratios are per standard deviation."
#| eval: !expr have_model2
ft_check1_model2(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr have_model2
cat(check1_model2_note(res), "\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model2-dropped
#| tbl-cap: "Person-years the model could not use. Nothing here is imputed."
#| eval: !expr have_model2
ft_check1_model2_dropped(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr have_nested
cat("**Against the baseline.** ", check1_nested_note(res), "\n", sep = "")
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr no_model2
cat("> **No Model 2.** ", res$meta$model2_note, "\n", sep = "")
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="default" icon=false}
## What this model can and cannot say here

On simulated data this is **machinery, not a finding** --- and that holds
whichever way the ratio comes out. Exit in this simulation is a rule applied
to the language score, and how closely content achievement tracks that score
is a parameter of the generator. Whatever this table reports, it is reporting
the generator's own design back. It is not evidence that any state's exit
process is or is not selecting on achievement. Run against a real delivery,
the same table is a genuine test.

Read it as evidence about *selection*, not about students: a ratio away from
1 says the exit process is responding to something beyond the language test,
which is a fact about the policy as implemented.
:::

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr have_type3
cat("### Additional check: the non-ELP criterion\n\n",
    "This state's exit rule uses a criterion beyond the ELP score, so it ",
    "enters the model alongside it. ", res$type3_covariate$caption, "\n",
    sep = "")
```

## The weighting index (experimental)

::: {.callout-warning appearance="default" icon=false}
## Not an established statistic

What follows is a **candidate** the Process Overview sketches, not a
validated method: retention share as a hard floor, selection strength as a
continuous downweight above it. It has not been tested against real data,
nothing in this package uses it, and no decision should rest on it until it
has been checked against the Indiana pipeline.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-weights
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate grade weights. Experimental: shown to be pressure-tested, not used."
#| eval: !expr have_weights
ft_check1_grade_weights(res)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
#| eval: !expr have_weights
s <- res$selection_strength
if (!is.na(s$value)) {
  cat(sprintf(paste0("Selection strength is %s, computed as %s. It is a ",
                     "single number for the whole cohort here; a per-grade ",
                     "version needs an interaction or a refit at each grade ",
                     "and is not built.\n"),
              format(round(s$value, 3)), s$basis))
}
```

## Looking at

Discrete-time survival analysis applied to one entry cohort: students who
entered EL status in the same grade, in the same year, tracked forward across
subsequent grades. Two models are named here because the rest of the process
refers back to them.

**Model 1 --- the unconditional survival model.** How long students stay in
EL status, with nothing held constant. It comes in two parts, and they answer
the same question in different registers. The *descriptive* part is the life
table, the curves and the at-risk estimate: no predictor at all, only counts
of who was at risk, who exited and who was lost, with the split by initial
band a way of grouping students rather than a variable in a model. The
*fitted* part runs in two steps: first the odds of exiting in each year in
status with no covariate at all, which is the life table written as a model;
then the same thing with the student's entry score added. Neither involves
achievement data.

**Model 2 --- the ELA-augmented survival model.** The second of those with
lagged content achievement added, to test whether academic performance is
doing selection work that is supposed to belong to the language test alone.
Model 1 is what it is compared against, which is why all three are fitted.

Every covariate in these models is measured **before** the exit decision it
is used to predict --- fixed at entry, or lagged a year. The current year's
language score is what the exit rule is applied to, so including it would
restate the rule rather than test anything, and would strip Model 2 of its
ability to answer the question it exists for.

## Looking for

From Model 1: the shape of the time-to-exit distribution --- the typical
number of years students take to exit, what share of the cohort exits within
the state's ESSA-expected timeline, and what share appears never to exit,
still EL-classified many grades later.

## Interpreting it

Model 1 tells you the descriptive shape of your state's exit patterns ---
when, whether, and after how long students are likely to exit under current
policy and practice. That is useful in its own right, independent of whether
the current threshold sits at the right level: it sets realistic expectations
and gives you plain-language material for talking with stakeholders about
what a typical EL trajectory looks like in your state.

Two cautions carry the weight here.

**Column F, and the curve drawn from it, are a lower bound** --- not a
completion rate. Students who disappear from the data are censored, not
non-exiters: we stop being able to observe them, which is not evidence that
they stayed in status. The final row is the window's edge --- there is no
following year in which an exit could be observed, so B is empty and everyone
still classified is censored there.

**Read the band split as a description, not a prediction.** A cohort that
starts higher exiting sooner is what the exit rule is built to produce; it
says nothing on its own about whether the threshold sits at the right level.
The bands near the exit threshold hold very few K entrants --- a student
screening at the threshold would not have been identified --- so those bands
suppress, and that is the design working, not a gap in the data.

**No average time in status appears anywhere in this document**, because on
censored data it is not defined. The honest summaries are the median years to
exit and the share exiting within the timeline, both of which arrive in a
later pass.

::: {.callout-important appearance="default" icon=false}
## Caution: remember your data structure

This cohort is students who started in `r res$meta$start_grade`. The total
exit numbers and percentages across *all* students who exit after each grade
will be different, because later entrants --- including newcomers arriving in
the upper grades --- are not in this table at all. Read it as the trajectory
of one entry cohort, never as the state's overall exit rate.
:::


## What is not here

Check 1 is complete: the life table, the exit curves, the survival estimate
and its median, the timeline outcomes, both fitted models and the
experimental index all render above. Four things are deliberately absent.

**A confidence interval on anything but the estimate.** The life table's own
columns are counts, and the observed cumulative share is a count against a
denominator that includes students nobody is following any more. Only the
at-risk estimate is an estimator, and only it is banded.

**A per-grade selection strength.** The index uses one ratio for the whole
cohort. The Process Overview asks for it at each grade, which needs either an
interaction term or a refit through each grade; neither is built, and the
single number should not be read as if it were per grade.

**Any mechanical use of the index.** It is rendered to be pressure-tested
against real data, starting with the Indiana pipeline. Nothing downstream
consumes it.

**Later start grades.** This is one K cohort. Students entering in grade 4,
or in grade 9 as newcomers, have different trajectories, and the deck's own
next step is to repeat the analysis for them one starting grade at a time.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="default" icon=false}
## Decide before moving on

How much weight later grade-level findings can carry, based on Model 1 and
Model 2 together.

The Process Overview sketches a candidate two-part index for making that call:
*retention share* --- at each grade, what fraction of the original entry
cohort is still EL-classified, and so still at risk --- as a hard floor,
following the same logic as the minimum-N suppression thresholds already used
in this pipeline; and *selection strength* --- how far Model 2's lagged-ELA
hazard ratio sits from 1 --- as a continuous downweight above that floor. A
grade can fail on either count independently: thin-but-unselected data, or
well-populated-but-heavily-selected data.

That index is **an untested proposal, not an established statistic**. It is
flagged here as something to build and pressure-test against real data before
it is presented to an SEA audience as anything more than a candidate idea, and
nothing in this package uses it mechanically.
:::
